# Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study

### Abstract

Extremal constructions play a central role in the design and analysis of algorithms. Integrality-gap instances expose the limitations of relaxations, while hard configurations reveal the structural sources of computational difficulty. Such constructions, however, are still typically discovered by expert researchers through a slow and largely manual process. This paper investigates how machine learning can accelerate their discovery and thereby support algorithm design and analysis. We build on PatternBoost, a recent framework that alternates local search with generation from a trained transformer and has shown promise in finding mathematical constructions. We use its Explorer implementation to investigate three problems: integrality gaps for maximum independent set of rectangles, integrality gaps for stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, and hard instances for recursive guillotine cutting. By exploring a range of representations of candidate constructions, the local search operations used to modify them, and the surrogate model used to rank candidates before exact verification, we carefully adapt the framework to these combinatorial geometry problems.

While naive representations and search strategies fail to find non-trivial instances, our tailored adaptation discovers numerous non-trivial constructions. For stabbing unit squares, the method reaches a gap of 20/13≈1.54, which improves on the best known lower bound of 3/2 in the literature. Purely automated search converges rapidly and then plateaus, prompting the question of what is required to push the bound higher still. We find that the diversity of the initial instance set plays an important role. With modest expert

input in the form of a structured staircase construction, the system reaches an improved integrality gap of 14/9≈1.555. These results demonstrate that machine learning and domain expertise can be combined to discover new extremal constructions that advance algorithmic lower-bound evidence.

### 1 Introduction

Extremal constructions are a central driver of progress in algorithm design and analysis. An integrality-gap instance exposes the limits of a relaxation by separating its value from the true optimum; a hard configuration reveals why a class of algorithms cannot go further. Such constructions identify the structural obstacles that any successful algorithm must overcome, and they often become the starting point for new theory. For computational geometry problems, progress has repeatedly depended on a single carefully crafted construction. Yet these constructions are still usually found by expert researchers through a slow, manual, and problem-specific process.

This paper asks whether machine learning can accelerate the discovery of such extremal objects. We build on PatternBoost [11], a recent framework that alternates local search with generation from a transformer trained on high-scoring candidates, using its Explorer implementation [3]. Applying this framework to combinatorial geometry is far from automatic. Candidate objects have rich geometric structure, and a single combinatorial object has many coordinate encodings, since translating, reflecting, rotating, or slightly perturbing it without changing which objects overlap leaves the objective unchanged. The true objective itself often requires solving a difficult optimization problem; and the learner only succeeds if the representation exposes the relevant combinatorial signal. We therefore redesign the three components that determine the effectiveness of the search: the representation of candidate objects, the local search operations, and the surrogate model used to rank candidates before exact verification.

<tbc>forms of extremal construction in combinatorial geometry. For the maximum independent set of rectangles, we seek instances where a natural relaxation substantially overestimates the size of the largest pairwise disjoint subfamily of rectangles. For stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, we seek configurations where the fractional stabbing number is significantly smaller than the minimum number of horizontal and vertical lines needed to stab all squares. For recursive guillotine cutting, we seek configurations that are difficult for algorithms restricted to recursively partitioning the instance by guillotine cuts.

A direct application of the pipeline fails. Naive representations and generic local search rediscover only trivial constructions or stall at the smallest, easiest gap instances. After tailoring the pipeline to the geometry and combinatorics of the problems, however, the system discovers non-trivial constructions for all three problems. For unit-square stabbing, the fully automated system reaches a gap of 20/13≈1.54, exceeding the best known lower bound of 3/2 for the problem. For MISR and guillotine cutting, the constructions found (3/2 and 1/3) do not improve on the best known bounds (Section 3); for these two problems the contribution lies in the method and its analysis rather than in new extremal objects.

Our experiments show that this success depends on co-design. We systematically vary the representation, local search, and surrogate components across the three problems, and independently verify every reported construction. No single component is sufficient on its own, and the best construction is rare in the design space: for each problem, only one of the 27 configurations we tried reaches its best value, so obtaining it demands careful exploration of the component choices.

Pure automation, however, has a clear limit. The search improves rapidly and then plateaus well before its time budget is spent, and simply running it longer does not move it further. Analyzing the learning dynamics, we find that the plateau is one of reachability: within a fixed search setup the automated loop cannot leave the region it starts in. This leads to a human-in-the-loop strategy: use domain expertise not to hand-design the final construction, but to recast the problem in a structured formulation in which the extremal obstruction is close to native. For unit-square stabbing this is a staircase construction that lifts a one-dimensional family of intervals to unit squares by products. With this modest expert input, the unit-square stabbing gap increases further to a certified value of 14/9≈1.555, _improving on the best known lower bound of_ 3/2 _by a wider margin still._

These results support a broader view of machine<tbc>

<tbc>learning as a partner in algorithm engineering. The role of the model is not to replace mathematical insight, but to amplify it: exploring large construction spaces, identifying promising patterns, and allowing expert guidance to be applied where it is most valuable.

In summary, we contribute:

1. an adaptation of PatternBoost, through its Explorer implementation, to extremal construction discovery in combinatorial geometry. The adaptation includes problem-specific representations, local search operations, and surrogate models. This turns a pipeline that finds only trivial instances into one that discovers exactly verified constructions, including a 20/13≈1.54 integrality gap for unit- square stabbing that improves on the best known lower bound of 3/2;<tbc>

2. a systematic ablation study across three pipeline components and three target problems, with independent verification of every certificate, showing that representation, search, and surrogate ranking must be co-designed: for each problem, only one of the 27 configurations reaches its best value; and<tbc>

3. an analysis of the plateau reached by purely automated search, together with a human-in-the-loop strategy based on an expert-structured staircase construction. This strategy raises the unit-square stabbing gap further to 14/9≈1.555, exceeding the prior best known lower bound and demonstrating productive collaboration between machine learning and domain expertise.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 surveys model-guided construction search, machine learning for combinatorial optimization, and instance-hardness methods. Section 3 defines the three problems and their exact objectives. Section 4 describes the PatternBoost/Explorer framework. Section 5 explores the design space of components and presents the constructions found, including the unit-square result that beats the best known bound. Section 6 reports the human-in-the-loop staircase construction. Section 7 concludes and outlines future directions, and Section 8 covers reproducibility.

## 2 Related work

### 2.1 Model-guided construction discovery

A growing body of work uses machine learning to search for explicit mathematical constructions. Wagner showed that a reinforcement-learning method, the deep cross-entropy method, can produce explicit constructions and counterexamples to conjectures in extremal<tbc>

<tbc>combinatorics and graph theory [35]; despite considerable engineering effort, however, we could not get this method to generate non-trivial geometric configurations. AlphaTensor used deep reinforcement learning to discover matrix-multiplication algorithms that improved on Strassen’s construction for the first time in over fifty years [15]. FunSearch pairs a large language model with an automatic evaluator to search over programs, and improved the best known bounds for the cap-set problem and for online bin packing [30]. AlphaEvolve extends learning-guided discovery to broader scientific and algorithmic tasks [27]. PatternBoost alternates classical local search with a transformer trained on high-scoring candidates [11]. We build directly on PatternBoost, through its Explorer implementation [3]. In contrast to existing work, our candidates are geometric objects whose exact score is itself an optimization problem, which calls for carefully designed surrogates to guide the search. A complementary line of work settles extremal questions by complete search, most prominently SAT solving, and emits machine- checkable certificates, as in the resolution of the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem [20]. We share the insistence on independently verifiable certificates, but replace exhaustive search with learning-guided generation of geometric objects.

### 2.2 Machine learning for combinatorial optimization

This research area has received significant attention in the last decade with a large body of work. We refer the interested reader to the surveys by Bengio et al. [5], Cappart et al. [7], and Wang et al. [36]. This literature mostly learns to _solve_ instances, through learned branching, cutting, or heuristic acceleration, whereas we use learning to _generate_ extremal instances. The generation of extremal instances cannot be easily formulated as a solvable optimization problem: the objective we maximize is itself the output of an exact optimization, an LP and an ILP, so it cannot be predicted directly by a learned model. While some instance representations can be borrowed from this literature, the model here only proposes candidate instances, each of which is then scored by an exact solver, so every gap we report is an exact, independently computed value rather than a model estimate.

### 2.3 Instance hardness and adversarial instance generation

Searching for configurations that are hard for an exact objective places our task in the instance-hardness and instance-space literature. In this context, there has been work on instance-space analysis and the evolution<tbc>

<tbc>of discriminating test instances [32], principled measures of instance difficulty [31], methodologies and open challenges for understanding instance hardness [33], and the evolution of combinatorial instances that are difficult to solve [34]. Our work can be read as automated hard-instance discovery, with the distinction that every reported instance carries an exact, independently re-verifiable certificate.

### 2.4 Human-guided discovery and diversity- driven search

Two lines of work inform our human-in-the-loop strategy. The first is human-guided machine discovery: Davies et al. show that machine learning can guide expert mathematical intuition toward new results [13], and machine discovery and expert refinement can compound, as when human mathematicians rapidly improved on AlphaTensor’s machine-found matrix-multiplication schemes [21]. Our staircase construction is in the same spirit: the expert does not hand- build the answer but recasts the problem into a structured formulation in which the extremal obstruction is native, and the learned search then tunes it to exceed a known lower bound. The second is quality-diversity search, which deliberately maintains a diverse population rather than optimizing a single objective: novelty search abandons the objective in favor of behavioral novelty [24], and MAP-Elites illuminates a search space by retaining the best solution in each region of a feature space [26]. These ideas motivate the diversity controls that let the automated search reach its strongest fully automated construction, and the quality-diversity archive we propose as future work.

## 3 Problems and exact objectives

For this study, we consider three combinatorial geometry problems - maximum independent set of rectangles (MISR), unit-square stabbing, and guillotine cutting. Next, we describe the three problems and the best known upper and lower bounds for them.

### 3.1 MISR integrality gap

In the MISR problem, we are given a finite family R of closed axis-parallel rectangles and we seek the maximum number of pairwise-disjoint rectangles. Let \(\alpha(\mathcal{R})\) denote this integer optimum and let \(\alpha^*(\mathcal{R})\) be the optimum of the standard point (equivalently clique) LP relaxation [8], which assigns \(x_R\ge 0\) to each rectangle subject to \(\sum_{R\unknown p}x_R\le 1\) for every point _p_. Because axis- parallel rectangles have Helly number two for pairwise intersections, this equals the clique relaxation of the<tbc>

rectangle intersection graph. The score is

\(\mathrm{score}_\mathrm{MISR}(\mathcal{R})=\frac{\alpha^*(\mathcal{R})}{\alpha(\mathcal{R})}.\)

Informally, MISR asks for the largest subfamily of pairwise-disjoint rectangles, and a difficult instance is one whose clique-LP optimum \(\alpha^*\) substantially exceeds the integer optimum \(\alpha\). Figure 1 (left) shows a small instance together with a maximum independent set.

Deciding MISR, and the corresponding covering problem, is NP-complete \[17\]. A long line of work has developed approximation algorithms: Adamaszek and Wiese gave a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) for the weighted problem \[2\], and Chuzhoy and Ene obtained an asymptotically faster QPTAS \[12\], while Mitchell gave the first polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for unweighted MISR \[25\], later improved to a 3-approximation by Gálvez, Khan, Mari, Mömke, Pittu, and Wiese \[18\].

The quantity we search over is the integrality gap of the clique-LP relaxation, for which lower and upper bounds are known. Chalermsook and Chuzhoy gave a polynomial-time _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation by rounding this relaxation, which also shows that its integrality gap is at most _O_(loglog_n_) \[8\]; a simpler _O_(loglog_n_)- approximation was subsequently given by Chalermsook \[9\]. On the lower side, Chalermsook and Chuzhoy constructed rectangle families whose clique-LP integrality gap is asymptotically at least 3/2 \[8\], and Caoduro, Cslovjecsek, Pilipczuk, and Wegrzycki proved essentially tight bounds for axis-parallel segments, exhibiting families whose gap tends to 2 \[6\]. Since axis-parallel segments are a degenerate special case of axis-parallel rectangles, these families carry over, so the gap for rectangles can likewise be driven arbitrarily close to 2. In summary, the best known bounds on the clique-LP integrality gap are an upper bound of _O_(loglog_n_) \[8\] and a lower bound approaching 2 in the limit \[6\]; the value 2 is a supremum over growing families rather than a gap realized by any single finite instance. Our search targets finite instances of fixed, small size, for which the largest gap realizable is a different and generally smaller quan<tbc>

<tbc>tity than these asymptotic limits; the certificate stores rectangles, the intersection graph, maximal cliques, an optimal integral independent set, LP primal and dual values, and solver status.

## 3.2 Unit-square stabbing integrality gap

In the unit-square stabbing problem, we are given a finite family S of axis-parallel unit squares, and we seek the minimum number of axis-parallel lines that together intersect every square. A horizontal or vertical line stabs a square if it intersects it. Let L(S) be the finite set of critical lines obtained by taking one representative per interval cell induced by the square-side coordinates. Because the set of squares a line stabs changes only when the line crosses a square edge, all lines whose coordinate lies in the same cell stab exactly the same squares, so this compression is exact: it reduces the infinitely many candidate lines to a finite universe while leaving both the integer and the fractional stabbing optima unchanged. Let \(\tau(\mathcal{S})\) be the minimum number of axis-parallel lines stabbing all squares, and \(\tau^*(\mathcal{S})\) the optimum of the set-cover LP over L(S). The score is

\(\mathrm{score}_\mathrm{stab}(\mathcal{S})=\frac{\tau(\mathcal{S})}{\tau^*(\mathcal{S})}.\)

Informally, the goal is to pierce every square with as few horizontal and vertical lines as possible, and a difficult instance is one whose set-cover LP optimum \(\tau^*\) is much smaller than the integer optimum \(\tau\). Figure 1 (middle) shows a small instance and an optimal integer stabbing.

The rectangle stabbing LP relaxation has integrality gap exactly 2 for general rectangles \[19, 4\], and _e/(e_-1)≈1.582 for horizontal segments \[23\]. For unit squares, Elbassioni and Ray gave the best known bounds via threshold rounding: the integrality gap is strictly below 2, at most 1.9<o>3</o>, and at least 3/2, the lower bound coming from a four-square construction whose LP optimum is 2 but whose integer optimum is 3 \[14\]; they conjecture the true value is \((35-\sqrt{5})/20\approx 1.638\). The certificate stores square coordinates, the compressed critical-line universe, the incidence matrix, an optimal integer cover, LP primal and dual witnesses,<tbc>

and solver status.

### 3.3 Recursive guillotine hardness

In the guillotine cutting problem, we are given a finite family R of pairwise interior-disjoint axis-parallel rectangles in a bounding box, and we seek a recursive sequence of guillotine cuts that preserves as many rectangles as possible. A guillotine cut of a current box is a horizontal or vertical segment spanning the box; rectangles it crosses are destroyed and rectangles strictly on each side recurse. The recursion continues until every region contains at most one rectangle, and no separate bound on the number of cuts is imposed: since a cut can only destroy the rectangles it crosses, an optimal strategy never uses more than |R|-1 cuts. Let save(R) be the maximum number of rectangles preserved by an optimal recursive strategy. The score is

\(\text{score}_\text{guill}(\mathcal{R})=1-\frac{\text{save}(\mathcal{R})}{|\mathcal{R}|}.\)

Informally, one recursively slices the bounding box with full horizontal or vertical cuts, and a difficult instance is a packing from which every guillotine sequence must destroy a large fraction of the rectangles. Figure 1 (right) shows a small instance and the outcome of an optimal cutting sequence.

Guillotine separability and cutting sequences were studied by Pach and Tardos [28], Abed et al. [1], and Khan and Pittu [22]. The central quantity is the fraction of rectangles a guillotine sequence can separate. For general disjoint rectangles, Pach and Tardos showed that an \(\Omega(1/logn)\) fraction can always be separated and conjectured that a constant fraction always suffices [28]; this remains open. For squares the separable fraction is at least a constant: Abed et al. showed that some constant fraction can always be separated [1], and the best explicit guarantee was improved to 1/40 [22] and then to 9/256≈3.51% [10]. In the other direction, there is an arrangement of squares from which no guillotine sequence can separate more than half. The optimal constant for squares therefore lies between 9/256 and 1/2. Such separability bounds translate directly into dynamic-programming approximations for the corresponding independent-set problems. The exact verifier is a dynamic program over coordinate-induced rectangle-subset states; the certificate stores saved and destroyed counts, the optimal recursive cut tree, first- cut and threshold diagnostics, the DP state count, and solver status.

Each problem is scored by an exact objective computed by a verifier that is independent of the search, so that the exact score, and not a surrogate, is the value reported everywhere. Appendix A gives small, easily ver<tbc>

<tbc>ifiable instances that certify a non-trivial objective for each problem: an integrality gap above 1 for MISR and unit-square stabbing, and a destroyed fraction above 0 for guillotine cutting.

## 4 PatternBoost/Explorer framework

**The PatternBoost/Explorer loop.** PatternBoost [11] was recently proposed as a framework for discovering mathematical constructions with the help of a trained model. It alternates two phases over a growing database of scored constructions. In the _local-search_ phase, existing constructions are perturbed by small targeted moves and improved ones are kept; in the _global- learning_ phase, a transformer trained on the highest- scoring constructions in the database generates new candidates, which are handed back to local search. The transformer supplies globally informed starting points that local search alone would rarely reach, while local search supplies the correction that turns rough generated candidates into valid constructions; the combination outperforms either phase alone [11]. In principle, only the problem-specific scoring function needs to change between problems. However, we discovered in this work that the local search operation and the representation also need to be carefully engineered for each problem. Figure 2 shows the loop; pseudocode is given in Appendix F. It is a population-based search: each generation scores the population with the surrogate, exactly audits the elites at a fixed interval, periodically retrains a fresh model on the archive, and refills the population by mutating elites with the configuration’s local-search operator and adding a few random newcomers.

_The transformer._ A construction is serialized as a canonical JSON string and tokenized character by character, with start and end markers. The model is a decoder-only transformer that predicts the next token autoregressively and is trained by next-token cross-entropy on the elite database, so it learns the<tbc>

We deliberately keep it small and train it from scratch at every training event: two layers, four attention heads, embedding width 96, feed-forward width 384, GELU activation, no dropout, a causal attention mask, context length 128, and generated sequences of up to 512 tokens. It is optimized with AdamW at learning rate \(3\times 10^{-4}\), batch size 32, and three epochs per training call. The vocabulary is rebuilt from the current elite archive with explicit `\<BOS\>`, `\<EOS\>`, and `\<UNK\>` symbols, so there is no fixed global vocabulary size. Character- level tokenization keeps the vocabulary small at the cost of allowing malformed samples, which are discarded or repaired; when a training event yields too few parseable samples, an order-8 character _n_-gram model fitted to the same archive supplements the transformer output.

_The surrogate._ Each configuration carries a surrogate: a problem-specific function that ranks candidates within the search and selects the elite that will be exactly audited. Surrogates range from cheap structural statistics that never solve the objective, through approximations of it, to functions that invoke the exact scorer itself with additional shaping terms. A surrogate is therefore not necessarily an approximation: what separates it from the exact oracle is its role, since the oracle sits outside the search and alone determines reported scores.

_Local search and verification._ A local move makes a small, validity-preserving change to a construction, in the simplest case perturbing one coordinate by \(\pm 1\). The operations we use range from these simple coordinate perturbations to structure-aware moves and small, exactly scored hill climbs; the concrete operators considered for each problem are described in Section 5. Improved candidates are accepted greedily.

**Challenges in adapting to combinatorial geometry.** Adapting PatternBoost to combinatorial geometry is not automatic, because the geometric setting departs from the graph and sequence problems the framework was designed for in three ways. First, a construction is a set of geometric objects with large coordinate ranges and many symmetries - translation, reflection, and axis exchange - so a naive coordinate encoding represents each combinatorial structure in a great many equivalent ways and forces the transformer to spend its capacity relearning them. Second, the objective is not a closed-form count but the outcome of an exact optimization - an LP, an ILP and their ratio, or a dynamic program - which is expensive to evaluate and, being a ratio, changes only in coarse jumps, so most local moves leave it unchanged. Third, randomly generated or model-sampled coordinates rarely satisfy the validity constraints of a non-trivial instance, such<tbc>

<tbc>as disjointness, triangle-freeness, or congruence, so proposals must be repaired, and repair can silently undo a coordinated change. These difficulties are why the representation, the local-search operation, and the surrogate must be co-designed for each problem, which we take up in Section 5.

**Exact verification and certificates.** Trust rests on verification that is independent of the search. Before deduplication and scoring, candidates are canonicalized: coordinates are translated to a canonical origin, integer grids are scaled by their gcd when possible, objects are sorted by normalized coordinates or a canonical graph label, and ties are broken deterministically. Surrogates are allowed to be biased and problem-specific, but every reported value is recomputed by the exact oracle of Section 3 and saved as a standalone certificate. These oracles use only open-source solvers, with no commercial optimization license; the per-problem solvers and numerical settings are given in Section 5.2. To keep results non-trivial, accepted constructions required at least eight geometric objects, unit-square certificates required integer stabbing number at least four, and guillotine certificates required at least two destroyed rectangles. We disclose the strongest prior: one of the three guillotine representations builds its instances around a fixed seven-rectangle spiral obstruction topology, so the nine configurations using it search an obstruction family rather than neutral coordinates. It inserts neither a score nor a certificate, and our best guillotine construction does not come from it: the destroyed fraction of 1/3 is reached by the neutral `rect\_direct\_disjoint` representation, while the spiral-seeded configurations reach at most 0.27. A strict post-processing audit re-verified every construction, checking clean completion of every run, agreement among all recorded scores, certificate- hash consistency, and independent exact re-verification of every certificate. All runs terminated cleanly, and all 81 constructions passing the audit.

## 5 Exploring the design space of components for geometric construction discovery

### 5.1 Components

**The components and how we explore them.** The effectiveness of the search is governed by three components: the _representation_, which specifies how a construction is encoded and repaired; the _local-search operation_, which specifies how an encoded construction is changed; and the _surrogate_, which scores how promising each candidate is and ranks candidates for exact verification. For each problem we consider three choices of each component and explore every one of the resulting 27 combinations. Guided by the principle of shaping each component to the certificate being sought, the<tbc>

<tbc>choices for each problem range from direct coordinate encodings to structured encodings that build the target property into generation, from simple coordinate perturbations to exactly scored, structure-aware hill climbs, and from cheap graph or incidence statistics to surrogates that invoke the exact scorer during ranking.  1 lists all 27 choices.

**Components of the best configurations.** We describe in more detail the components that make up the best configuration for each problem.

For MISR, `triangle\_free\_rect` stores a list of integer rectangle coordinates under the constraint that the intersection graph stay triangle-free, that is, no three rectangles share a common point. Rectangles are added one at a time from a pool that mixes rectangles near existing ones, thin horizontal and vertical bars, and unrestricted random rectangles; a candidate is admissible only if its neighbors in the current intersection graph are pairwise non-intersecting, which is exactly what prevents a triangle. Repair deletes a member of any triangle that appears and refills to the minimum size. On this representation, `sequence\_pair\_pivot` (the local search) samples add, replace, nudge, resize, and delete moves with add and replace upweighted, drawing new rectangles from a large triangle-free pool. The surrogate `exact\_lp\_gap\_pressure` calls the full MISR exact scorer for every candidate it ranks and orders the population primarily by the exact clique-LP-to-integer gap \(\alpha^*/\alpha\), breaking ties in favor of a larger triangle- free lower bound. It is the most expensive MISR signal, since each ranking call solves the optimization exactly, same as the verifier.

For unit-square stabbing, `sqstab\_exact\_grid` stores distinct integer lower-left anchor endpoints and one common integer side length. Canonicalization removes translation and duplicates, so the exact critical-line universe is easy to regenerate and audit. `symmetry\_crossover\_hillclimb` is an operator shared by all three problems that makes 25 exactly scored proposals per call, drawn as about 55% one- step shifts, 25% random relocations, 10% pairwise exchanges (swapping the vertical intervals of two objects), and 10% planar symmetries. Every proposal is repaired and exactly scored; acceptance is gated first by a non-triviality requirement (here, a candidate needing at least four lines is preferred) and then by the exact objective, and only non-worsening proposals are kept. `exact\_stab\_gap\_pressure` calls the exact set- cover and fractional-LP scorer for each candidate and ranks primarily by \(\tau/\tau^*\), with small tie-breaks that prefer a larger integer cover, a smaller fractional optimum, and a more spread-out LP support.

For guillotine cut, `rect\_direct\_disjoint` initial<tbc>

<tbc>izes by turning random grid cells into disjoint unit rectangles, a deliberately neutral start that usually yields an easily separable packing; repair removes interior overlaps, refills to the minimum size, and canonicalizes, leaving the local search to grow the simple cells into long bars and interlocking packings. `witness\_breaking` first finds an easy witness, a guillotine-separable subset of majority size (enumerated for small _n_, sampled otherwise), and then tries to destroy that separation by extending a rectangle across a projection gap or inserting a thin bridging rectangle, alongside bar replacement, cut blockers, and motif copies. `depth\_limited\_dp` runs the recursive-cut dynamic program to depth four, optimistically treating every rectangle still present at the depth limit as saved, and ranks by the implied destroyed fraction; it sees past the first cut while staying cheaper than the full dynamic program, but misses obstructions that surface deeper than four levels.

## 5.2 Experimental setup

**Experimental design.** For each problem the three components are crossed fully, giving 27 configurations, and the three problems together give 81. Each configuration repeatedly generates or repairs a population in its representation, scores novel candidates with its surrogate, exactly audits the elite at a fixed interval and saves a certificate only when the exact score strictly improves, mutates the elite with its local-search operation, and periodically trains a freshly initialized transformer on the strongest archive entries and samples new candidates from it, with a character _n_-gram sampler filling any shortfall of parseable samples. Every configuration is run once, from freshly generated geometry, with no repeated-seed axis and no warm-started certificate, under an identical 24-hour wall-clock budget. To attribute an effect to a single component we use its _marginal mean_, the average exact score over the 9 configurations that share that component choice. Because there is one run per configuration, these marginals are descriptive summaries rather than estimates with error bars.

**Hardware and run cohorts.** Experiments ran on compute nodes built from AMD EPYC 7742 processors at 2.25 GHz with 128 cores and 480 GB of RAM each (about 3.75 GB per core). Each configuration was dispatched as one array task requesting four cores and 16 GB of RAM. All configurations shared exact elite scoring every five generations, 16 requested model samples per successful training event, per-generation checkpointing, an application budget of 86,400 seconds, and a safety cap of 1,000,000 generations; the runs were thus both time-bounded and iteration-capped, but every reported configuration stopped on the time<tbc>

<tbc>budget and none reached the iteration cap. The set of 81 configurations combines three runtime cohorts rather than one common population and elite setting: 36 rows used object count _n_=8 on a grid of 8 with population 32, elite 6, and training every seven generations; 42 rows used _n_=12 on grid 8 for MISR and guillotine and _n_=20 on grid 16 for unit-square stabbing, with population 16, elite 4, and training every ten generations; and the final three unit-square rows used _n_=20 on grid 16 with population 32, elite 12, an initial pool of 128 candidates, and four fresh immigrants per generation.

**Initialization.** Every run starts from fresh pseudorandom geometry rather than an injected certificate, and the random seeds are retained only for provenance and replay. Initialization is problem- andrepresentation-specific. MISR uses integral rectangle coordinates: at grid 8, repaired lower endpoints lie in 0-9 and upper endpoints in 1-10, and the quadratic- program representation draws its initial coefficients from \[-4,4\]. Unit-square instances place congruent squares whose anchors lie in 0-8 at grid 8 and 0-16 at grid 16; the exact-grid representation samples a common integer side from 1 to 4, while the fixed-symmetry representation fixes the side at 2. Guillotine populations in the direct representation choose disjoint unit grid squares from an \(8\times 8\) grid, the random fixed packing uses a dynamic domain of side at least max(grid+2, 2_n_), and the recursive-obstruction representation randomizes core spacings and orientation and adds filler rectangles. The evidence therefore points to the geometric search landscape, not transformer capacity, as the binding constraint, and the compact transformer is the better use of a fixed compute budget.

## 6 Human-in-the-loop: an expert-structured staircase construction

**Structuring the search space.** The diagnosis of Section 5 is that the automated loop is confined to the region it starts in. Much of the reason is _what it samples_: the neutral search draws square coordinates directly, and among independently placed squares a coupled, provably hard pattern of square-line incidences is<tbc>

<tbc>astronomically unlikely to arise. This is where a human enters the loop, not to hand-build the final construction but to change what the search samples. For unit- square stabbing the vehicle is a _staircase_ construction: squares are never sampled independently but generated as products \(I\times J\) of intervals from a one-dimensional family, which forces exactly the shared-line incidences that make stabbing hard, and the local moves become scans over the interval starts, the common length, the level count and assignments, the support points, and shifted staircase variants, in place of coordinate jitter on squares. A line-stabbing lower bound then follows from a proof template on the one-dimensional part, as we now describe.

**The staircase formulation.** _One-dimensional interval layer._ The construction begins with a finite ordered set of rational support points \(P=\{p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_m\}\subset\mathbb{Q}\) and a rational probability measure \(\mu:P\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}\) with \(\sum_{p\in P}\mu(p)=1\). A candidate specifies a common interval length _L_ and a finite family of intervals \(\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}_0\sqcup\mathcal{I}_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\mathcal{I}_{q-1}\) partitioned into ordered _levels_; every interval has the same length _L_ after<tbc>

<tbc>scaling, and only the starting positions and level labels vary. For each level _r_ the verifier computes a certified lower bound

\(a_r\le min_{I\in\mathcal{I}_r}\mu(I\cap P),\)

the minimum one-dimensional measure captured by every interval in that level. The search variables are the interval starts, the level assignments, the common length, and the support weights that make these inequalities strong.

_Product lift to squares._ The two-dimensional family is formed by products: for \(I\in\mathcal{I}_r\) and \(J\in\mathcal{I}_s\) the square \(Q_{I,J}=I\times J\) is included whenever the level pair is admissible, that is, whenever \(a_r+a_s\ge 1\) for the relevant pairs (_r,s_) below the target threshold. Because _I_ and _J_ share the length _L_, each _Q<sub>I,J</sub>_ is an axis-parallel unit square after a uniform rescaling. A vertical line _x=t_ meets _Q<sub>I,J</sub>_ exactly when \(t\in I\), and a horizontal line _y=t_ exactly when \(t\in J\), so stabbing the squares reduces to hitting the interval family on each axis.

_Lower-bound certificate._ Fix a target integer _T_. For any split into _u_ vertical and _v_ horizontal lines with _u+v\<T_, the staircase levels are arranged so that the vertical lines miss some interval \(I\in\mathcal{I}_r\) and the horizontal lines miss some interval \(J\in\mathcal{I}_s\) with (_r,s_) admissible. The square _Q<sub>I,J</sub>_ is then present and unstabbed, so no set of fewer than _T_ lines can stab the whole family, which proves \(\tau(\mathcal{S})\ge T\). The fractional optimum \(\tau^*(\mathcal{S})\) is computed by the standard LP over the compressed critical-line universe, and the construction is tuned so that \(\tau(\mathcal{S})/\tau^*(\mathcal{S})=14/9\).

**The difficulty of producing structure.** The reason such structure has to come from a human is that the obstructions that force a large gap are hard to manufacture automatically. For unit-square stabbing, a neutral coordinate search must invent both the geometry and its proof of hardness at once from raw square positions; the staircase formulation removes that double burden. The same difficulty recurs, often more sharply, elsewhere: for MISR a large gap wants a dense conflict structure, for which a high chromatic number of the intersection graph is a natural proxy, yet rectangle intersection graphs of chromatic number 5 or 6 are rare and delicate to build while random ones are almost always low-chromatic, so neither hand construction nor uniform sampling readily supplies them. Expert structure such as the staircase is valuable precisely because it makes these otherwise- elusive obstructions native to the search space.

**Interpretation.** Modest expert input, supplied precisely where the automated loop stalls, is enough to surpass the best known lower bound for unit-square stabbing, producing a construction that neither the automated search nor the expert reached alone. The same complementarity appears downstream of the search as well as upstream of it: manual post-processing reduces the automated 20/13 witness from twenty squares to eleven without changing its score, and the 3/2 MISR construction extends by hand into an infinite family. In each case, the search supplied a seed that a human could compress or generalize.

## 7 Conclusion and future directions

Extremal constructions are still found largely by hand. We showed that a learning-guided search can find them automatically, provided the representation, local search, and surrogate are designed together: it reaches a gap of 3/2 for MISR, a destroyed fraction of 1/3 for guillotine cutting, and 20/13≈1.54 for unit-square stabbing, the last exceeding the best previously known lower bound; the staircase formulation raises it to 14/9≈1.555. Every construction carries an independently re-verified certificate. Two lessons follow: good configurations are<tbc>

<tbc>isolated in the design space, so no component succeeds alone, and automated search plateaus for a structural rather than a computational reason, since it cannot leave the region it starts in.

Three directions follow from the plateau. An archive organized by structural features rather than by score would retain candidates that score poorly today but carry the seeds of a better construction; composition operators that combine certified obstructions while preserving their ratio would let a small witness be scaled rather than rediscovered; and the exact structure our solvers already compute - LP duals for MISR, incidences for stabbing, cut trees for guillotine hardness - could guide moves directly. The pipeline applies to any extremal question with an exactly computable, certifiable objective [29, 16]. The division of labor that works is across human and machine: the search covers ground that would be tedious by hand, the expert supplies the template it cannot invent.

<tbc>`exact\_grid` stores distinct integer lower-left anchors and one common integer side length, with initial anchors sampled without replacement from a grid and the initial side drawn from 1 to 4. Canonicalization removes translation and duplicates and keeps a common side, so the exact critical-line universe is easy to regenerate and audit. It is the least indirect of the three square representations, searching the actual coordinates and scale, at the cost of a large, rugged space with many plateaus. `fixed\_symmetry\_grid` stores distinct grid anchors at a fixed object count and a fixed common side (two in the final runs), reduced over all translations and the eight symmetries to a canonical coordinate list. Cardinality and side length are restored after every proposal, which makes representation comparisons clean at a fixed scale but prevents the search from moving between side-length regimes.

_Local-search operations._ `coord\_mutation` moves one square by at most one grid step, duplicates a nearby square, or deletes one. Representation-specific additions matter: with the incidence layout it can copy another square’s _x_- or _y_-coordinate; with the exact grid it also has line tightening, canonical shifting, a random restart, and a guided neighbor selector; and with the fixed- symmetry grid, fixed-count repair restores cardinality and re-canonicalizes. It is a plain coordinate mutation only in its simplest pairing. `sqstab\_local\_hillclimb`<tbc>

<tbc>augments the base moves with stabbing-aware proposals: copying or tightening a square onto another’s coordinate (optionally offset by the side length), adding or replacing a unique anchor, dropping a square, shifting to the origin, or restarting with fresh grid points and a resampled side. After the first proposal it builds a few nearby candidates and, for families up to about 48 squares, keeps the one with the best exact stabbing key; above that size it switches to the cheap greedy-cover- versus-frequency proxy to control cost. `symmetry\_ crossover\_hillclimb` uses the same 25-proposal shift, relocate, exchange, and symmetry portfolio, exactly scored. Acceptance is gated first by a nontriviality requirement - a candidate needing at least four lines is preferred to one with a smaller integer cover - and then by the exact gap; within the gate only nonworsening proposals are kept. The gate is an explicit search preference, not a target ratio or injected construction.
